analysis.one_liner: Lets US antitrust law target drug makers for charging Americans more than foreign buyers.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Judiciary Committee without a vote, a cosponsor, or any action after its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would treat a drug maker's sales to foreign wholesalers as if they happened in the US under the Clayton Act, the antitrust law that bans charging different buyers different prices. In practice, this would let US wholesalers and consumers sue when manufacturers charge far less to wholesalers abroad than at home. The goal was to narrow the gap that left Americans — especially seniors — paying roughly 43% more than Canadians for the same medicines.
analysis.who_benefits: American consumers, particularly seniors who pay cash for prescriptions, would gain the most. The bill's findings cite the General Accounting Office's estimate that US consumers pay on average 43% more than Canadians for the same drugs, and note seniors crossing the border to buy cheaper medicines. If enforced, the threat of price-discrimination lawsuits would push manufacturers to narrow the gap between US and foreign wholesaler prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors and consumers paying cash for prescriptions

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Clayton Act so that price discrimination between US wholesalers and foreign wholesalers is deemed to injure competition, giving US buyers a legal claim against manufacturers that sell the same drug much cheaper abroad.

The bill's findings cite GAO data that Americans pay on average 43% more for prescription drugs than Canadians, and note that many seniors cross into Canada or Mexico to buy the same US-made drugs at lower prices.
Because foreign sales would be deemed US sales for enforcement purposes, manufacturers could no longer isolate their lower foreign prices from US antitrust scrutiny.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear the cost, either by facing price-discrimination lawsuits, by narrowing US-foreign price gaps, or by raising foreign prices to equalize. Foreign consumers could also face higher prices if manufacturers equalized upward.

drawbacks.text: The remedy is indirect: rather than capping prices, it relies on antitrust lawsuits, which are slow and uncertain, so relief for consumers would be delayed and uneven.

Drug makers argued generally that international price differences reflect other governments negotiating prices down below cost, and that forcing price parity could lead manufacturers to raise foreign prices or reduce US market revenue available for research and development — a cost an honest supporter would have to weigh.
The bill's own findings concede that other countries should pay a larger share of drug development costs, meaning a US-only remedy shifts the debate over who funds research rather than resolving it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real, documented problem — Americans paying an average 43% more than Canadians for the same medicines — but chose an indirect antitrust route rather than direct price relief, so the benefit to consumers would have depended on litigation and manufacturer behavior. It was also a one-sponsor bill with no cosponsors and no committee action, so it was never tested in debate. On paper it leaned clearly toward consumers and against pharmaceutical pricing practices, but as drafted it offered more pressure than guaranteed relief.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2000 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never took it up before Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Helen Chenoweth-Hage introduced the Prescription Drug Fairness Act on July 18, 2000, as the 106th Congress entered its final months.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action was recorded: no hearings, no markup, no floor vote, and no cosponsors ever joined.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers came out ahead, since the bill's death preserved their ability to charge US buyers more than foreign wholesalers. American consumers, especially seniors paying high prescription prices, gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Helen Chenoweth-Hage
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made the case in its findings that Americans pay 43% more than Canadians for the same drugs.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 18, 2000 and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Henry Hyde
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; it sat without action for the rest of the session.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never attracted a vote or a cosponsor from either party — one Republican sponsored it, zero members joined, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record.

industries.note: The bill would expose their practice of selling the same drugs to foreign wholesalers at far lower prices than to US wholesalers to price-discrimination suits, pressuring them to narrow the gap. Their gain under the status quo is the higher prices American consumers, especially uninsured seniors, pay.

US wholesalers paying more than their foreign counterparts for identical drugs would gain a legal claim under the amended Clayton Act, and any price relief could pass down to pharmacies and consumers.
